John Bradford
JON BRAD-ferd
proper noun / person
English surname from a place-name meaning broad ford; John from Hebrew Yochanan, “the LORD is gracious.” Preacher and Marian martyr (c. 1510–1555).

📖 Biblical Definition

John Bradford was an English preacher of rare tenderness and steel, converted under the Reformation's light and made a powerful instrument for the gospel in London. Known for deep humility—tradition remembers his cry at the sight of a condemned man, There but for the grace of God goes John Bradford—he held free grace without soft antinomianism. Under Mary he was imprisoned and at last burned at Smithfield in 1555. His letters from prison still speak of Christ's sufficiency, patient suffering, and love to the brethren. Bradford's combination is the church's need in every age: doctrine clear enough to die for, and a heart soft enough to weep for sinners. He did not trade the gospel for safety, nor zeal for cruelty. In an age that either weaponizes doctrine or dissolves it into mood, Bradford's ashes preach again: hold Christ, hate your own pride, and be ready to lose the world rather than the truth. Grace made him lowly; grace made him bold; both are required of gospel men.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

English Reformation preacher and Marian martyr, burned at Smithfield in 1555; remembered for gospel clarity and deep humility.

expand to see more

JOHN BRADFORD, English Protestant preacher and martyr (c. 1510–1555).

Powerful gospel preacher in London under the Edwardian Reformation.

Imprisoned under Mary I; burned at Smithfield in 1555.

Remembered for humility and prison letters full of Christ.

Often linked with the saying on grace contrasted with a condemned man's estate.

📖 Key Scripture

1Co 15:10 — "But by the grace of God I am what I am: and his grace which was bestowed upon me was not in vain; but I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me."

Eph 2:8-9 — "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast."

Php 1:29 — "For unto you it is given in the behalf of Christ, not only to believe on him, but also to suffer for his sake."

2Ti 1:8 — "Be not thou therefore ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner: but be thou partaker of the afflictions of the gospel according to the power of God."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Cheap grace talk keeps Bradford's humility slogan and drops his martyrdom; true grace produces both lowliness and courage.

expand to see more

The first corruption is to reduce Bradford to a proverb about luck. His point was grace, not chance. The second corruption is harsh orthodoxy without his tears. He held truth and tenderness together. A third soft form is prison-letter romanticism without present faithfulness under smaller costs.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of Bradford's name. The principle to recover is grace that humbles the preacher and steadies him at the stake.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Bradford embodies Reformed gospel preaching under the English Reformation's fire.

expand to see more

Edwardian reform — London preaching under Protestant advance.

Marian persecution — imprisonment and death at Smithfield, 1555.

Humility — grace-conscious self-knowledge before God.

Letters — prison counsel full of Christ and patience.

Martyr company — with Hooper, Latimer, Ridley, and the English witnesses.

Usage

"John Bradford was burned at Smithfield in 1555."

"He preached free grace with humility and courage."

"His prison letters still feed suffering saints."
